clue.text: Departs with booze in barrel

indicators.note: 'with' means accompanied by, so one piece simply joins on to the next

blocks.note: D is the timetable abbreviation for departs
rum is a spirit, an example of booze

explanation.surface: Someone leaves the bar carrying liquor stored in a cask.
explanation.walkthrough: D for departs is the abbreviation used on railway timetables.
explanation.definitionFit: A drum is a cylindrical container for liquids, so it serves as a synonym for a barrel or cask.

clue.text: Poor Scots, upset about good dress

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over, so in a down entry the letters run bottom to top
'about' means around, so one piece goes round another

blocks.note: puir is the Scots spelling of poor
G is the standard abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Impoverished Scots are upset over having to put on smart clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scots' is not people here but the language: the Scots word for poor is PUIR, which turns over to RIUP and wraps round G.
explanation.definitionFit: To rig up someone is to kit them out or clothe them, an informal verb meaning to dress.

clue.text: One’s trapped in large unknown religious building

indicators.note: something trapped in a space is held inside it, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: monster as an adjective means huge
a means one, as in a single thing
y is an algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: Someone is stuck inside a vast mysterious church.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after One is 'is': one is trapped in MONSTER, then Y follows. MONSTER as an adjective (a monster hit) means large.
explanation.definitionFit: A monastery is the residence of a community of monks, a building given over to religious life.

clue.text: Have a second job - flash working followed by rest

indicators.note: 'followed by' places one piece straight after the other in reading order

blocks.note: a mo is a moment, as is a flash
a machine that is working is on
to light on something is to come to rest upon it, like a bird alighting

explanation.surface: Advice for a worker taking on extra shifts: a burst of activity, then a break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flash' tempts you towards MOON (to bare one's bottom), but it is MO, a moment. Light here is the verb meaning to settle on, as birds alight.
explanation.definitionFit: To moonlight is to work a second job, typically secretly or in the evenings beyond regular employment.

clue.text: Friend increasingly a mess after one leaves

indicators.note: whatever leaves is no longer there, so a letter drops out

blocks.note: more mucky, the comparative of a word for messy
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A companion becomes ever more of a shambles once someone moves out.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove I from MUCKIER to leave MUCKER.
explanation.definitionFit: Mucker is informal British slang for a close mate or pal, so it is a colloquial synonym.

clue.text: Certain to abandon Society after blatant offer

indicators.note: to abandon something is to leave it behind, so a letter is dropped
'after' puts one piece later than another in the down reading

blocks.note: overt means open and unconcealed
sure means certain
S is the abbreviation for Society

explanation.surface: A sure bet to leave high society after a brazen proposition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Certain' is not an adjective on the offer: it is the word that loses its S. In a down clue, 'after' puts that remnant beneath.
explanation.definitionFit: An overture is an approach or proposal made to open negotiations, a noun synonym for an offer.

clue.text: Language school in Gothenburg offering a restricted range

indicators.note: a restricted range shows only part of what is there, so the letters sit within a longer run

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, the whole second word, and the start of the city

explanation.surface: A Swedish language school whose course options are limited.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs through schoo-L IN GO-thenburg; 'school' is part of the fodder, not a definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Lingo is an informal, often jocular word for a foreign tongue or jargon, a colloquial synonym.

clue.text: Intermediary, grand one, working to secure venture supported by our group

indicators.note: working material is being reshaped, so these letters are rearranged
to secure is to hold firmly, so one piece holds others inside
in a down entry, being supported means sitting above, so one piece comes before the next

blocks.note: G is short for grand, a thousand
taken as written, then rearranged
to venture money is to bet it
we is the group that includes us

explanation.surface: A middleman, a big player, works to win backing for a business venture from our team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grand one' looks like a phrase but splits: grand is the thousand, and 'one, working' is the rearranged word that splits open to hold the venture. 'Supported by' means above, as this is a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A go-between carries messages or negotiates between two parties, the same role as a mediator.

clue.text: Herbal flavouring not currently for you and me

blocks.note: thy is the old-fashioned possessive meaning belonging to you, no longer in current use
taken as written

explanation.surface: A seasoning that isn't right for us just now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not currently' marks an archaism: THY is the old word for your.
explanation.definitionFit: Thyme is an aromatic garden herb whose leaves are used to season cooking.

clue.text: Wesley, say, to lose relish, we hear, for Pope’s name

indicators.note: what we hear is speech, so the spelling may differ from the sound

blocks.note: John Wesley founded Methodism; 'say' marks him as an example of the name
to pall is to become tiresome or lose its appeal

explanation.surface: A Methodist leader goes off his food in a story about papal naming.
explanation.walkthrough: Wesley is an example of a JOHN; pall, to stop pleasing, is pronounced like PAUL.
explanation.definitionFit: John Paul was the regnal name chosen by two twentieth-century popes, including John Paul II.

clue.text: Encores rang out - from this part of church?

indicators.note: 'out' suggests letters set loose from their order, free to be reformed

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Calls for more music resounded through the church, perhaps from up in the loft.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue nods at music: the encores ring out from where the organ stands.
explanation.definitionFit: An organ screen is the partition between nave and choir in many churches, on which the organ sits.

clue.text: Tree bark

blocks.note: first meaning: the laurel whose leaves flavour stews
second meaning: to howl like a hound

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tree bark' reads as the outer layer of a trunk; instead, both words are separate meanings, a tree and a dog's howl.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names the laurel tree and also the deep, prolonged howling of hunting dogs.

clue.text: Drop off surface

blocks.note: first meaning: to doze briefly
second meaning: the raised pile on fabric such as velvet

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like something falling from a surface; 'drop off' is falling asleep, and the surface is the pile on cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers a short sleep taken during the day and the fuzzy raised fibres on textiles.

clue.text: Driven by courage to pin down constant source of feminine attraction?

indicators.note: pinning something down holds it in place, so one piece is gripped inside another
'by' means beside, so the pieces stand next to each other

blocks.note: driven means sent, as when a person is driven mad
c is the constant for the speed of light
bottle is British slang for nerve or courage

explanation.surface: A man is spurred by his nerve to pin down the woman who keeps attracting him.
explanation.walkthrough: c is the physicist's constant, the speed of light. Bottle meaning courage is British slang: to lose your bottle is to lose your nerve.
explanation.definitionFit: A scent bottle holds perfume, which a woman might wear to be alluring, hence the question mark.

clue.text: British author showing increasing cunning?

blocks.note: first meaning: a bestselling English novelist and former Tory politician, Jeffrey by first name
second meaning: the comparative of arch, meaning sly

explanation.surface: A British novelist turns out to be ever more crafty.
explanation.walkthrough: Arch means sly or knowing, so 'more arch' is the second sense; the question mark flags this playful reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Jeffrey Archer is a bestselling English novelist, and the comparative of arch means slyer still.

clue.text: Actor with judo moves getting religious role?

definitions.note: names the person holding a church role

indicators.note: a move shifts things to new positions, so these letters are set in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A performer lands a part as a monk thanks to his martial arts skills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moves' looks like a noun belonging to judo, but it is the signal to rearrange both words.
explanation.definitionFit: A coadjutor is a bishop appointed to assist a diocesan bishop, often with succession rights.

clue.text: Theatrical magician favouring twirling ropes

indicators.note: twirling spins things round, so these letters end in a different order

blocks.note: pro means in favour of
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A stage conjuror likes his rope tricks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Theatrical' points to a play: the magician is from Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: Prospero is the exiled duke and sorcerer at the centre of Shakespeare's The Tempest.

clue.text: Playwright’s written about offender’s handicraft

indicators.note: 'about' means around, so one piece is written round another

blocks.note: George Bernard Shaw, the Irish dramatist
crim is short for criminal, with the possessive s

explanation.surface: A dramatist has written about the crafts made by a prisoner.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after Playwright stands for 'is'; the one on offender's stays as a letter. Crim is informal shorthand for criminal.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrimshaw is the carving or engraving of whalebone and ivory, traditionally by sailors, a kind of folk art.

clue.text: Irish nationalist, once on revolutionary lines

indicators.note: a revolution turns things over, so these letters are overturned into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written, to be rearranged
L is the abbreviation for line, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: An Irish nationalist who once followed revolutionary principles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' sits well with a nationalist, but it signals the rearrangement of the two preceding words.
explanation.definitionFit: Daniel O'Connell, called the Liberator, campaigned for Catholic emancipation and repeal of the union with Britain.

clue.text: Tree left above a stream? I’m not sure

indicators.note: in a down entry, being above means coming earlier in the reading

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for left
taken as written
a burn is a Scottish word for a small stream
um is the sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: Someone unsure whether a tree grows beside the brook.
explanation.walkthrough: BURN for a stream comes from Scotland and northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: Laburnum is a small ornamental tree with drooping yellow flowers and poisonous seeds.

clue.text: Nonsense writer penning start of poem, getting positive response - a regular occurrence

indicators.note: the start of a word is only its opening letter
to pen is to enclose, so one piece is written inside another

blocks.note: Edward Lear wrote nonsense verse such as The Owl and the Pussycat
the opening letter of the word
yea is an old word for yes

explanation.surface: A writer of limericks starts a poem and gets an approving reply, as happens often.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward Lear is the classic nonsense poet. 'Regular' is fair because the extra day comes round at a fixed interval.
explanation.definitionFit: A leap year comes every fourth year, an event recurring on a fixed calendar schedule.

clue.text: English person, unwelcome overseas? Smile and depart

blocks.note: a grin is a broad smile
to go is to leave

explanation.surface: Advice to an unwelcome English tourist abroad: smile and leave.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition describes how the word is used rather than offering a strict synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Gringo is a disparaging Latin American term for a foreigner, especially an English speaker.

clue.text: No choice in limitations on game for former King

indicators.note: limitations are boundaries, so only the outer edges of the word are kept

blocks.note: the edge letters of the word
a choice is this or that; a choice between two identical things is no choice at all
the same edge letters again, the second option

explanation.surface: A deposed king was left with no options within the rules of the game.
explanation.walkthrough: The edges of game give GE; offered a choice of GE OR GE, you have no choice at all. A playful, almost cryptic-definition construction.
explanation.definitionFit: Six British kings have been called George, the last of them dying in 1952.

clue.text: Jack, losing heart in summer is conflicted, accepting university later - the attraction of Amsterdam?

indicators.note: losing the heart means the central letters go
something conflicted is torn and disordered, so these letters are rearranged
to accept is to take in, so one letter goes inside the rest

blocks.note: the word with its two middle letters removed
taken as written, to be rearranged
U is the abbreviation for university
gives no letters: it says this letter goes in after the rearranging is done

explanation.surface: A man called Jack is torn over a summer trip, then takes in a university town, perhaps Amsterdam.
explanation.walkthrough: JK joins SUMMER IS in the rearrangement; 'later' says U is slotted in after that step.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rijksmuseum is the Dutch national museum in Amsterdam, home to Rembrandt's Night Watch and a major tourist draw.

clue.text: Quantity of paper covering lecturer’s field of study

indicators.note: a covering goes over and around, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: a ream is 500 sheets
L is the abbreviation for lecturer

explanation.surface: A stack of paper hides an academic's area of research.
explanation.walkthrough: REAM wraps L; the 's after lecturer is 'is' grammar for the surface only.
explanation.definitionFit: A realm can mean a sphere or domain of activity or knowledge, like a discipline.

clue.text: Whole account identifying Middle Eastern shrub

blocks.note: a sum is a total, the whole amount
AC is the abbreviation for account

explanation.surface: A full report naming a plant from the Levant.
explanation.walkthrough: SUM plus AC; 'identifying' just joins wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sumac is a shrub whose dried red berries make a tangy spice in Levantine cooking.

clue.text: Not entirely compassionate relationship

indicators.note: not entirely means incomplete, so the last letter is cut off

blocks.note: caring and compassionate

explanation.surface: A caring person's bond with someone, though the kindness is only partial.
explanation.walkthrough: KIND loses its final D.
explanation.definitionFit: Kin can mean kinship, a family connection or blood tie between people.

clue.text: Is no longer addicted to excitement

blocks.note: first meaning: gives up a habit, as in breaking a drug habit
second meaning: thrills, as in doing something for the buzz

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one sentence about quitting thrill-seeking; split it after 'to'.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to overcome a habit, and the plural noun means thrills sought for pleasure.

clue.text: Function needing no initial skill

indicators.note: with no initial the opening letter is gone

blocks.note: a part is a role or function

explanation.surface: A job that requires no prior ability.
explanation.walkthrough: PART loses its P.
explanation.definitionFit: Art can mean a craft or knack acquired by practice, as in the art of conversation.

clue.text: ‘Style’ included in version of a normal description of Queen?

indicators.note: a version is a reworked form, so these letters are reordered
something included in another is placed within it

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
chic is elegance or style

explanation.surface: A fashion writer slips the word style into an ordinary account of the Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: A NORMAL is rearranged round CHIC. The question mark admits the definition is a description rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Monarchical means relating to a monarch, an adjective that would apply to a reigning sovereign.

clue.text: Additional people arrived besieging British coastal resort

indicators.note: besiegers surround a place, so one piece encircles another

blocks.note: more means extra or additional
came means arrived
B is the abbreviation for British

explanation.surface: Extra crowds turn up and lay siege to a British seaside town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'British coastal resort' reads as one phrase, but British is the inserted letter. 'People' is surface padding. Morecambe is a seaside town on the Lancashire coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Morecambe is a Lancashire seaside town on the bay of the same name, a classic holiday destination.

clue.text: Astute, in the old way

blocks.note: first meaning: sagacious, shrewd
second meaning: an archaic noun for manner

explanation.walkthrough: 'In the old way' reads as 'traditionally', but it means an archaic word for way; together with 28 across it makes the comedy duo Morecambe and Wise.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means sagacious, and the obsolete noun meant manner, surviving in phrases like 'in any wise'.
